messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: problem with latent variables
parts: I suspect that it has something with not enough obseration (40)
Yup, that would be a problem.
and the binary data which is the explanatory variables for the latent variable
You need to declare the names of binary / ordinal variables when you call sem(..., ordered = c("V","F")), unless those variables are already stored as type "ordered" in the data frame.

first model

model <- "
R=~a1*(V+F)
C~a2*R
A ~ a3*R

P ~ a4*R+a5*A
C ~ a6*A+a7*P
"

The line in red doesn't work the way (I believe) you intend it.  I am guessing that you want to constrain the factor loadings of V and F to equality, using the same label.  Notice in your output that the variable F does not appear anywhere.  You need to specify that equality constraint by repeating the same label for both indicators:

R =~ a1*V + a1*F

The distributive property of multiplication does not apply to a1*(V + F) because you aren't doing multiplication.  It is just an operator in the model syntax for applying a label to a value.

second model

model <- "
R=~a1*V+b1*F
C~a2*R
A ~ a3*R

P ~ a4*R+a5*A
C ~ a6*A+a7*P
"

This model is not identified.  Your latent variable only has 2 indicators, so the equality constraint in model 1 is necessary for identification.  Either equate the 2 loadings and fix the factor variance to 1 using sem(..., std.lv = TRUE), or fix both loadings to 1 and estimate the factor variance:

R =~ 1*V + 1*F

You might need to constrain thresholds, too, but I don't think that is necessary.

Terry

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: problem with latent variables
parts:
model <- "
R=~a1*V+b1*F
C~a2*R
A ~ a3*R

P ~ a4*R+a5*A
C ~ a6*A+a7*P
"
fit <- sem(model, data = nivsem,ordered = c("V","F"),std.lv = TRUE)

This model is still not identified.  You need to constrain the 2 factor loadings to be equal by giving them the same label.  With continuous indicators, that is sufficient to just-identify the scale of the construct, but I am unsure whether it is sufficient with categorical indicators (since you need to set the scale of the normal variables assumed to underlie the ordered categorical observed indicators, in addition to the scale of the latent construct).
Thanks for all the effort! I am probably doing stupid mistakes, I'm very new in field of SEM...

Sorry I can't be of more help, but it is difficult to tell whether your problems are just due to using WLS with such an unthinkably small sample size for that estimator.  40 is even small for ML with normally distributed variables.

Terry

> <http://std.lv> = TRUE)*

> This model is still not identified.

I think the model is identified in theory. But we are unlucky with the
sample.

I tried simulating data with a large sample size, and it runs just fine:

set.seed(12345)
pop.model <- '
R =~ 1*V + 0.6*F
V | -0.5*t1
F | +0.5*t1
C ~ 0.5*R
A ~ 0.7*R
P ~ 0.6*R+0.9**A
C ~ 0.2*A+0.3*P
'
Data <- simulateData(pop.model, sample.nobs = 10000)

model <- '
R =~ a1*V + b1*F
C ~ a2*R

A ~ a3*R

P ~ a4*R+a5*A
C ~ a6*A+a7*P
'

fit <- sem(model, data = Data, ordered = c("V","F"), std.lv = TRUE)

Since we only have N=40, I would suggest avoiding the latent variable
'R' altogether, and construct some sort of an observed variable based on
V and/or F.

Yves.
